stories.title: Salesforce Acquires Cresta for a Reported $2.7B; Ada Merges with Dialpad — Three Agent Vendors Exit Independence in One Week
stories.body: On November 2, 2026, Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire Cresta, a voice-first AI platform for contact centers whose customers include Marriott, Comcast, and Alaska Airlines; the reported price is $2.7 billion. Two days later, Dialpad and Ada announced they are merging to build what they call an 'agentic operating system for customer work,' combining voice, customer intelligence, and AI agents. Enterprise communications analyst Dave Michels described the moment as 'The Big Blender,' with both deals signalling that enterprise communications, CX, and AI are converging into larger platform stacks.
stories.why: Three named competitors — Cresta, Ada, and Intercom Fin (already acquired by Salesforce in June 2026 for ~$3.6B) — are now inside or beside Salesforce's Service Cloud, making Salesforce the dominant consolidated incumbent a Graas seller will be measured against on nearly every enterprise CX deal. The consolidation redraws the shortlist retailers will bring to vendor reviews: independent best-of-breed agents are disappearing, which is both a threat (Salesforce bundle) and an opening (Salesforce lock-in concerns create room for a focused alternative).
stories.source_label: Salesforce Newsroom / CX Today / Yahoo Finance

stories.title: McKinsey 'State of AI 2026': 32% of Enterprises Cancelled a Software Purchase to Build With Agents — But Profit Impact Stuck at 37%
stories.body: McKinsey's State of AI 2026 report, published August 25 and drawn from 1,719 respondents across 97 countries, found that 32% of organizations decided against buying at least one software product or feature because they could build it in-house with agentic coding tools. Among large enterprises (revenue >$1B), 40% are now scaling AI agents in at least one function, up from 27% the year before. Despite the activity surge, the share of organizations reporting any EBIT impact from AI stayed flat at 37%, and only 6% qualify as high performers attributing at least 5% of EBIT to AI.
stories.why: The build-vs-buy flip is the objection a Graas seller will hear in every discovery call with a CIO — 'we can just build this.' McKinsey's own data provides the counter: building is rising but ROI is not, which means the gap lies in data infrastructure and context, not code — exactly what Graas addresses. Use the 40%-scaling / 37%-profit-impact tension to reframe the conversation from 'should we build agents' to 'what do agents need to actually work.'

stories.title: Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Cancelled by End of 2027; 70% of Vendor-Built Agents Abandoned by 2028
stories.body: Gartner issued two enterprise AI predictions that have circulated widely in Q4 2026: first, that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, aligning with observed enterprise abandonment patterns; second, that 70% of enterprises will abandon agentic AI built by vendor forward-deployed engineering by 2028. Separately, Forrester's mid-2026 assessment found that most 'agentic' experiences deployed today are still conversational, with humans still driving decisions and checkout in the vast majority of cases. Both firms point to missing data foundations — not weak models — as the primary reason pilots stall.
stories.why: Gartner's cancellation rate gives a Graas seller a credible, named-analyst number to anchor the 'why pilots fail' narrative: enterprises are launching agents without the governed context layer underneath them. The Forrester finding that most deployments are still just chatbots reinforces that the gap between demo and production is a data-architecture problem, not a model problem — which is exactly the gap Graas closes.

stories.title: BCG: CPG Leader Shifts Replenishment to Agentic Planning, Cuts Out-of-Stocks; Walmart Running Multi-Agent Supply Chain in Production
stories.body: BCG's May 2026 Executive Perspectives paper 'From Copilots to Enterprise' documents a global CPG company that redesigned replenishment using agentic AI — shifting from periodic planning to daily, SKU-level inventory optimization through a multi-agent architecture. Separately, a Deloitte Insights research piece published in March 2026 confirmed that Walmart is already running a unified multi-agent supply chain architecture in production. BCG frames the shift as moving from functional optimization to enterprise decision orchestration, with agents simultaneously improving effectiveness and efficiency in ways no prior planning tool could.
stories.why: A named CPG replenishment deployment with BCG's fingerprints, plus a Walmart production confirmation, gives sellers two proof points that retail and CPG agents in ordering and supply chain are real and in production — not lab experiments. When a prospect says 'agents aren't ready for our supply chain workflows,' these are the reference cases to anchor the counter.
stories.source_label: BCG Executive Perspectives / Deloitte Insights (via evolvancemarketresearch.com)

stories.title: Sierra Reaches $400M+ ARR at $15.8B Valuation, Serves 40%+ of Fortune 50 on Outcome-Based Pricing — and Is in Talks for a $20B Round
stories.body: Sierra, the enterprise customer-service agent platform co-founded by Bret Taylor, reported ARR exceeding $400 million by October 2026, up from $150 million in early 2026 and $100 million in late 2025, and is in talks to raise a new round at a $20 billion valuation. The company says it now serves more than 40% of the Fortune 50, charges on outcome-based pricing rather than per seat or per message, and in November 2026 announced that browser-automation specialist Anon is joining the company to extend agents into secure web navigation. Competitor Decagon, which raised $250 million in January 2026 at a $4.5 billion valuation, is estimated at roughly $35 million ARR — placing Sierra at a commanding scale lead among pure-play agent vendors.
stories.why: Sierra's ARR trajectory and Fortune 50 penetration make it the most credible benchmark a retail buyer will cite when evaluating agent vendors — sellers need to understand its outcome-pricing model, its Context Engine architecture, and where its gaps are (deep multi-system retail data context) to position Graas alongside or against it. The Anon acquisition signals Sierra is moving toward autonomous browser-based workflows, which could expand its footprint into retail ordering and operations use cases that Graas already owns.
stories.source_label: The CODEW / Silicon Valley Invest Club / aissist.io
